content: Monerans, or organisms classified under the kingdom Monera, are primarily bacteria and other microscopic, single-celled organisms. These organisms are characterized by their genetic material, which is not enclosed within a nucleus but instead exists freely within the cell. In contrast, the genetic material of plants, animals, and other eukaryotes is contained within a well-defined nucleus. Historically, Monera was considered one of the five biological kingdoms. However, advancements in molecular biology have revealed that Monera actually comprises two distinct domains: Bacteria and Archaea. Organisms within the Monera kingdom were defined by their prokaryotic cell structure, meaning they lack a nucleus. For this reason, the kingdom was sometimes referred to as Prokaryota or Prokaryotae. Recent analyses of DNA and RNA sequences have demonstrated that Bacteria and Archaea, the two major groups of prokaryotes, are not closely related to each other. In fact, they are as distinct from one another as they are from eukaryotes. This discovery led to the division of Monera into the domains Bacteria and Archaea, which are now part of the six-kingdom and three-domain classification systems. Modern classification schemes have abandoned the Monera kingdom entirely, treating Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya as separate domains or kingdoms. Before the five-kingdom model, organisms now classified as Monera were grouped into two divisions of plants: Schizomycetes (bacteria), which were considered fungi, and Cyanophyta (blue-green algae). Cyanophyta, now known as cyanobacteria, are recognized as a group of bacteria and are not closely related to plants, fungi, or animals. Carl Woese, based on molecular phylogeny studies, proposed in 1990 that prokaryotes (monerans) should be divided into two separate groups: Bacteria and Archaea. Woese's phylogenetic model, which roots all three domains (Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya) in a universal common ancestor, is widely accepted today. The most modern interpretation of this classification is the Universal and Eukaryote Phylogenetic Tree, based on 16S rDNA, as presented in the Tree of Life Web Project. Eubacteria (true bacteria) and Archaebacteria (archaea) differ significantly in the environments they inhabit. Eubacteria include the majority of bacteria that interact with humans, such as Escherichia coli and species of the genus Salmonella. In contrast, Archaebacteria thrive in extreme environments, such as acidic hot springs and deep subsurface regions beneath Arctic ice. These groups were later renamed Bacteria and Archaea, which can sometimes cause confusion, as the term bacteria in common usage originally referred to all prokaryotic microorganisms, including monerans. Traditionally, organisms were classified into three categories: animal, vegetable, or mineral, as outlined in Systema Naturae. After the advent of microscopy, efforts were made to classify microscopic organisms as either plants or animals. In 1866, Ernst Haeckel proposed a three-kingdom system, adding Protista as a new kingdom to include most microscopic organisms. One of the eight major divisions of Protista was called Moneres, which included known bacterial groups such as Vibrio. Haeckel's Protista kingdom also included eukaryotic organisms now classified as protists. However, it was later determined that Haeckel's Protista kingdom was too diverse to be considered a single kingdom. In 1969, Robert Whittaker proposed a five-kingdom system for classifying living organisms. Whittaker's system placed most single-celled organisms into either the prokaryotic Monera or the eukaryotic Protista. The other three kingdoms in his system were the eukaryotic Fungi, Animalia, and Plantae.
